fundamentals.summary: A container is an ordinary process on the host kernel, isolated with namespaces, limited with cgroups and given a layered root filesystem. Know where that isolation ends.
points: Containers share the host kernel; VMs boot their own. The image brings userspace only, so kernel ABI and CPU architecture must match (or be emulated).
Namespaces isolate what a process sees: PID, network, mount, UTS, IPC, user and cgroup. Docker creates no time namespace, so the clock and kernel are shared.
cgroups v2 limit what it uses: memory.max (hard limit, then OOM kill, exit 137), cpu.max (quota/period from --cpus), cpu.weight (relative shares) and pids.max.
overlay2 stacks read-only image layers under one writable container layer. Reads search upper then lower layers; writes copy the whole file up; deletions become 0/0 whiteouts.
The stack is CLI → dockerd → containerd → shim → runc. runc (the OCI runtime) creates the process and exits; the shim keeps it alive across daemon restarts.
The OCI defines the runtime, image and distribution specs, which is why images move between Docker, Podman, containerd and CRI-O.
Docker Desktop runs Linux containers in a VM, so bind mounts cross a file-sharing boundary while named volumes stay fast.
traps: `--cpus` is a time quota, not pinning: `nproc` and `free` inside the container still report host-wide values.
With --memory set and --memory-swap unset, a host with swap lets the container use the same amount again as swap.
Root in a default container is host UID 0 with fewer capabilities, not an unprivileged user, unless user namespaces are enabled.
